title: Introduce downstream timeout
description: Project: Introduce downstream timeout. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: A downstream service starts returning 500s or hanging, and your API threads pile up waiting for responses. Without timeout and circuit-breaker policies, a single slow dependency can cascade into a full outage. This lesson covers how to set timeouts, configure retries safely, and use circuit breakers to fail fast when a dependency is unhealthy.

items: No timeout on HTTP or database calls, causing threads to wait indefinitely
Aggressive retries that amplify load on an already struggling downstream
Missing fallback behavior when the dependency returns errors
Thread pool starvation under sustained high latency, making the entire app unresponsive
Timeout values that are longer than the load balancer or reverse proxy timeout, causing silent connection drops

terms.definition: A pattern that stops sending requests to an unhealthy dependency after a threshold of failures is reached, allowing it time to recover.
A situation where multiple clients simultaneously retry failed requests, overwhelming the recovering service.
Isolating resources such as thread pools or connection pools per dependency so one failing service cannot consume all capacity.
A maximum allowed duration for an operation; exceeding it triggers cancellation or a fallback path.
Signaling to upstream callers that the system is overloaded so they can slow down rather than queue indefinitely.

data.text: The safest default is a short timeout, no automatic retry, and an explicit fallback. Add retry only after you understand the failure mode. Retry is appropriate for transient network errors and 503s; it is not appropriate for 400s, 401s, or 409s. Retrying a failed write without idempotency guarantees can create duplicate records.

data.title: Polly timeout and retry policy
data.content: A defensive HTTP policy in ASP.NET Core using Polly:

items: Set timeouts shorter than every upstream timeout in the call chain
Use exponential backoff with jitter for retries to avoid synchronized retries
Configure circuit breakers with failure thresholds and recovery windows appropriate to the dependency SLO
Add fallbacks or graceful degradation for user-facing requests
Test policies with chaos testing or fault injection before relying on them

data.caption: Circuit breaker state transitions under request load
data.definition:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Closed
    Closed --> Open: Failure threshold exceeded
    Open --> HalfOpen: Recovery timeout elapsed
    HalfOpen --> Closed: Test request succeeds
    HalfOpen --> Open: Test request fails

    note right of Closed
        Normal operation.
        Requests pass through.
        Failures are counted.
    end note

    note right of Open
        Fast-fail all requests.
        Downstream is considered
        unhealthy.
    end note

    note right of HalfOpen
        Allow one test request.
        If it succeeds, close the
        circuit. Otherwise, reopen.
    end note

data.title: Timeouts must be end-to-end
data.text: If your API timeout is 30 seconds but the load balancer kills connections at 15 seconds, the client sees a connection drop rather than a timeout. Document and enforce timeout budgets across every hop in the request path.

items.question: What timeout should I use for HTTP calls?
items.answer: Start with 5 to 10 seconds for internal services and 2 to 5 seconds for external APIs. The exact value should be shorter than the caller's timeout to leave room for fallback logic. Measure actual p99 latency before deciding.

items.question: Should I retry on all 5xx errors?
items.answer: Retry on 503 Service Unavailable and occasionally 502 Bad Gateway. Do not retry 500 unless you know it is transient. Retrying 504 Gateway Timeout is risky because the downstream may have processed the request.

items.question: How do I test resilience policies without breaking production?
items.answer: Use fault injection in integration tests. Libraries like Polly.Testing and ASP.NET Core's TestServer let you simulate timeouts, 500s, and latency. Run these in CI on every PR that touches resilience code.

data.title: Add resilience to an existing HTTP client
data.description: Take an existing HttpClient call that has no timeout or retry. Add a timeout, exponential backoff retry, and circuit breaker. Explain the rationale for each value you chose.
steps: Measure current p95 and p99 latency for the dependency
Set timeout to 1.5x p99 with a hard ceiling of 10 seconds
Add retry only for timeout and 503 responses
Configure circuit breaker based on the dependency's error budget
Write a test that verifies the circuit opens after repeated failures
data.expectedOutcome: You should have a resilient client with documented timeout, retry, and circuit-breaker settings, plus a test that proves the behavior.

data.title: Summary
points: Timeouts protect thread pools and user experience
Retry only transient failures; retrying non-idempotent writes causes duplicates
Circuit breakers fail fast and let unhealthy dependencies recover
Test resilience policies with fault injection
Document the timeout budget across every service hop
data.takeaway: Resilience is not about preventing failures. It is about preventing failures from spreading. A senior engineer designs systems assuming every dependency will fail and ensures the blast radius stays bounded.
